claim: N,N, Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) can rapidly induce an extremely immersive state of consciousness characterized by vivid and elaborate visual imagery.
source: N,N, Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) can rapidly induce an extremely immersive state of consciousness characterized by vivid and elaborate visual imagery.
evidence: This is a general characterization of DMT's effects, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: DMT induces a spatio-temporal pattern of cortical activation (i.e. travelling waves) similar to that elicited by visual stimulation.
source: Consistent with our hypotheses, results revealed a spatio-temporal pattern of cortical activation (i.e. travelling waves) similar to that elicited by visual stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental EEG data comparing DMT and visual stimulation conditions.

claim: DMT significantly decreases typical top-down alpha-band rhythms of closed-eyes rest.
source: Moreover, the typical top-down alpha-band rhythms of closed-eyes rest were significantly decreased, while the bottom-up forward wave was significantly increased.
evidence: This is supported by EEG measurements showing changes in alpha-band activity.

claim: DMT significantly increases bottom-up forward waves.
source: Moreover, the typical top-down alpha-band rhythms of closed-eyes rest were significantly decreased, while the bottom-up forward wave was significantly increased.
evidence: This is supported by EEG measurements showing changes in forward wave amplitude.

claim: Psychedelics reduce the 'precision-weighting of priors', thus altering the balance of top-down versus bottom-up information passing.
source: These results support a recent model proposing that psychedelics reduce the 'precision-weighting of priors', thus altering the balance of top-down versus bottom-up information passing.
evidence: This is a theoretical model supported by the experimental findings and references to prior work.

claim: DMT occurs endogenously in several organisms including humans, albeit in trace concentrations.
source: N,N, Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is a mixed serotonin receptor agonist that occurs endogenously in several organisms (Christian et al., 1977; Nichols, 2016) including humans (Smythies et al., 1979), albeit in trace concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When administered intravenously, DMT's subjective effects have a rapid onset, reaching peak intensity after about 2–5 min and subsiding thereafter, with negligible effects felt after about 30 min.
source: Administered in this way, DMT's subjective effects have a rapid onset, reaching peak intensity after about 2–5 min and subsiding thereafter, with negligible effects felt after about 30 min (Strassman, 2001; Strassman, 1995a; Timmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on DMT pharmacokinetics.

claim: Previous electrophysiological studies investigating changes in spontaneous brain function elicited by ayahuasca have reported consistent broadband decreases in oscillatory power.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies investigating changes in spontaneous (resting state) brain function elicited by ayahuasca have reported consistent broadband decreases in oscillatory power (Riba et al., 2002; Timmermann et al., 2019), while others have noted that the most marked decreases occur in α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) (Schenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The most marked decreases in oscillatory power under ayahuasca occur in α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz).
source: Previous electrophysiological studies investigating changes in spontaneous (resting state) brain function elicited by ayahuasca have reported consistent broadband decreases in oscillatory power (Riba et al., 2002; Timmermann et al., 2019), while others have noted that the most marked decreases occur in α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) (Schenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Alpha decreases correlated inversely with the intensity of ayahuasca-induced visual hallucinations.
source: Alpha decreases correlated inversely with the intensity of ayahuasca-induced visual hallucinations (Valle et al., 2016) and are arguably the most reliable neurophysiological signature of the psychedelic state identified to-date (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013) – with increased signal diversity or entropy being another particularly reliable biomarker (Schartner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study showing correlation.

claim: Alpha decreases are arguably the most reliable neurophysiological signature of the psychedelic state identified to-date.
source: Alpha decreases correlated inversely with the intensity of ayahuasca-induced visual hallucinations (Valle et al., 2016) and are arguably the most reliable neurophysiological signature of the psychedelic state identified to-date (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013) – with increased signal diversity or entropy being another particularly reliable biomarker (Schartner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents an inference from multiple studies.

claim: Increased signal diversity or entropy is a particularly reliable biomarker of the psychedelic state.
source: Alpha decreases correlated inversely with the intensity of ayahuasca-induced visual hallucinations (Valle et al., 2016) and are arguably the most reliable neurophysiological signature of the psychedelic state identified to-date (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013) – with increased signal diversity or entropy being another particularly reliable biomarker (Schartner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: In the first EEG study of the effects of pure DMT on on-going brain activity, marked decrease in the α and β (13–30 Hz) band power was observed as well as increase in signal diversity.
source: In the first EEG study of the effects of pure DMT on on-going brain activity, marked decrease in the α and β (13–30 Hz) band power was observed as well as increase in signal diversity (Timmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Increase in lower frequency band power (δ = 0.5–4 Hz and θ = 4–7 Hz) became evident when the signal was decomposed into its oscillatory component under DMT.
source: Increase in lower frequency band power (δ = 0.5–4 Hz and θ = 4–7 Hz) also became evident when the signal was decomposed into its oscillatory component.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study (Timmermann et al., 2019).

claim: Decreased alpha power and increased signal diversity correlated most strongly with DMT's subjective effects.
source: Decreased alpha power and increased signal diversity correlated most strongly with DMT's subjective effects – consolidating the view that these are principal signatures of the DMT state, if not the psychedelic state more broadly.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study (Timmermann et al., 2019).

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in cortical regions reveal distinct spatio-temporal dynamics during visual perception, which differ considerably from those observed during closed-eyes restfulness.
source: Focusing attention onto normal brain function, outside of the context of psychoactive drugs, electrophysiological recordings in cortical regions reveal distinct spatio-temporal dynamics during visual perception, which differ considerably from those observed during closed-eyes restfulness.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: These dynamics can be described as oscillatory 'travelling waves', i.e. fronts of rhythmic activity which propagate across regions in the cortical visual hierarchy.
source: It is possible to describe these dynamics as oscillatory 'travelling waves', i.e. fronts of rhythmic activity which propagate across regions in the cortical visual hierarchy (Lozano-Soldevilla and VanRullen, 2019; Muller et al., 2014; Sato et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Travelling waves can spread from occipital to frontal regions during visual perception, reflecting the forward bottom-up flow of information from lower to higher regions.
source: Recent results showed that travelling waves can spread from occipital to frontal regions during visual perception, reflecting the forward bottom-up flow of information from lower to higher regions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Top-down propagation from higher to lower regions appears to predominate during quiet restfulness.
source: Conversely, top-down propagation from higher to lower regions appears to predominate during quiet restfulness (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Halgren et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: During quiet closed-eyes restfulness a significant amount of backward waves spread from higher to lower regions.
source: Consistent with previous observations on independent data (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019), during quiet closed-eyes restfulness a significant amount of BW waves spread from higher to lower regions (as confirmed by a Bayesian t-test against zero for both DMT and Placebo conditions, BFs10 >>100, error <0.01%, 95% Credible Intervals (CI) DMT: [0.221, 0.637], Placebo: [0.273, 0.666])
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study and citation to previous work.

claim: During quiet closed-eyes restfulness no significant waves propagate in the forward direction.
source: whereas no significant waves propagate in the opposite FW direction (Bayesian t-test against zero: BFs10 <0.15, error <0.01%; 95% CI DMT: [−0.424, 0.088], Placebo: [−0.372, 0.110]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: After DMT injection, the amount of backward waves decreased but remained significantly above zero.
source: However, after DMT injection, the cortical pattern changed drastically: the amount of BW waves decreased (but remaining significantly above zero – BFs10 = 12.6, 95% CI: [0.057, 0.322])
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: After DMT injection, the amount of forward waves increased significantly above zero.
source: whereas the amount of FW waves increased significantly above zero (BF10 = 5.4 95% CI: [0.027, 0.336]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: The changes in travelling waves after DMT injection were not confounded by differences in dosage.
source: These results, obtained by comparing the amount of waves before and after injection (pre-post factor) of Placebo or DMT (drug factor), were confirmed by two Bayesian ANOVA performed separately on BW and FW waves (all factors including interactions reported BFs10 >>100, error <2%), and were not confounded by differences in dosage (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Power analysis comparing DMT and Placebo conditions after infusion for both forward and backward direction revealed values above 90%.
source: A power analysis comparing DMT and Placebo conditions after infusion for both FW and BW direction revealed values above 90% (FW case: μDMT=0.19, μPLACEBO = -0.20 and σ = 0.29 yields to power equals to 0.9168; BW case: μDMT = 0.18, μPLACEBO = 0.51 and σ = 0.25 gives power equals to 0.9205; in both cases, we considered a type I error rate of 5%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical power analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The changes in cortical dynamics appeared rapidly after intravenous DMT injection, and began to fade after about 10 min.
source: in-line with previous studies (Strassman, 1995a; Strassman, 1994; Timmermann et al., 2019), the changes in cortical dynamics appeared rapidly after intravenous DMT injection, and began to fade after about 10 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to previous work.

claim: Forward travelling waves increase during visual stimulation.
source: We recently showed that FW travelling waves increase during visual stimulation, whereas BW waves decrease, in-line with their putative functional role in information transmission (Pang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Backward waves decrease during visual stimulation.
source: We recently showed that FW travelling waves increase during visual stimulation, whereas BW waves decrease, in-line with their putative functional role in information transmission (Pang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Both forward and backward waves share a similar profile across DMT injection and visual stimulation conditions.
source: Remarkably, mutatis mutandis, both FW and BW waves share a similar profile across the two conditions, increasing and decreasing respectively following DMT injection or visual stimulation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from the current study and previous work.

claim: DMT produces an overall decrease in oscillatory power, specifically in the frequency band with the highest power values (i.e. alpha band).
source: If we consider the absolute (maximum) power values derived from the 2D-FFT of each map (i.e. before estimating the surrogates and the waves' net amount in decibel) as an estimate of spectral power, we can read the results reported in Figure 2C as an overall decrease in oscillatory power following DMT injection, more specifically in the frequency band with the highest power values (i.e. alpha band, but see next paragraph) (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013; Riba et al., 2002; Schenberg et al., 2015; Timmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: The decrease in oscillatory power induced by DMT is matched by a similar decrease induced by visual stimulation.
source: Such decrease in oscillatory power is also matched by a similar decrease induced by visual stimulation (all Bayesian t-test BFs10 >>100).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing DMT and visual stimulation conditions.

claim: Despite participants having their eyes-closed throughout, DMT produces spatio-temporal dynamics similar to those elicited by true visual stimulation.
source: These results demonstrate that, despite participants having their eyes-closed throughout, DMT produces spatio-temporal dynamics similar to those elicited by true visual stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Before DMT infusion, both forward and backward waves had a strong alpha-range oscillatory rhythm.
source: Before infusion, both FW and BW waves had a strong alpha-range oscillatory rhythm (Figure 3A, labeled 'PRE').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Following DMT injection, the waves' spectrum changed drastically, with a significant reduction in the alpha-band, coupled with an increase in the delta and theta bands, for both forward and backward waves.
source: Remarkably, following DMT injection, the waves' spectrum changed drastically, with a significant reduction in the alpha-band, coupled with an increase in the delta and theta bands, for both FW (δ-band: BF10 = 391.16, θ-band: BF10 = 19.23, α-band: BF10 = 16.04, β-band: BF10 = 0.64; all errors < 0.001%) and BW waves (δ-band: BF10 = 82.56, θ-band: BF10 = 30.58, α-band: BF10 = 549.54, β-band: BF10 = 1.43; all errors < 0.005%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: DMT induces an overall reduction in the amount of waves at each frequency, specifically in the alpha-band backward waves, but with the notable exception in the forward alpha band, in which DMT induces an increase in the waves' direction.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, and in agreement with previous analyses, DMT induces an overall reduction in the amount of waves at each frequency, specifically in the alpha-band BW waves, but with the notable exception in the FW alpha band, in which DMT induces an increase in the waves' direction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Forward waves tend to be weaker whenever backward waves are stronger, and vice versa.
source: This result demonstrates that, in general, FW waves tend to be weaker whenever BW waves are stronger, and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference from the negative correlation found in the data.

claim: Forward and backward waves remain present after drug injection, sum to a consistent total amount, and remain inversely related; it is only the ratio of contribution from each that changes after DMT.
source: In other words, FW and BW remain present after drug injection, sum to a consistent total amount, and remain inversely related; it is only the ratio of contribution from each that changes after DMT (i.e. less BW, more FW waves).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on wave correlations.

claim: There is a robust correlation between minute-by-minute intensity rates and the amplitude of the waves.
source: First, we found a robust correlation between minute-by-minute intensity rates and the amplitude of the waves, as shown in the first panel of Figure 5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The developing intensity of the drug's subjective effects and changes in the amplitude of waves correlate positively (forward waves) or negatively (backward waves) across time, both peaking a few minutes after drug injection.
source: This result reveals that the developing intensity of the drug's subjective effects and changes in the amplitude of waves correlate positively (FW) or negatively (BW) across time, both peaking a few minutes after drug injection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Around the moment where the drug had its maximal effect (2–5 min after injection), those subjects who reported the most intense effects were also those who had the strongest travelling waves in the forward direction, and the weakest waves in the backward direction.
source: Despite the limited number of data-points (n = 12), the correlation coefficients reach high values (~0.4), implying that, around the moment where the drug had its maximal effect (2–5 min after injection), those subjects who reported the most intense effects were also those who had the strongest travelling waves in the FW direction, and the weakest waves in the BW direction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on correlations.

claim: Ratings of all of the relevant questionnaire items correlated strongly with the increased amount of forward waves under DMT.
source: Finally, we correlated the amount of FW and BW waves with ratings focused specifically on visual imagery: remarkably, ratings of all of the relevant questionnaire items correlated strongly with the increased amount of FW waves under DMT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The same relationship between visual imagery ratings and waves was not apparent for the backward waves.
source: As the same relationship was not apparent for the BW waves, this consolidates the view that visionary experiences under DMT correspond to higher amounts of FW waves in particular.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cortical travelling waves (and increased forward waves in particular) correlate with the conscious visual experiences, whether induced exogenously (via direct visual stimulation) or endogenously (visionary or hallucinatory experiences).
source: Taken together with previous results from visual stimulation experiments independent of DMT (Pang et al., 2020), these data strongly support the principle that cortical travelling waves (and increased FW waves in particular) correlate with the conscious visual experiences, whether induced exogenously (via direct visual stimulation) or endogenously (visionary or hallucinatory experiences).
evidence: This is an inference combining current experimental data with previous research.

claim: Compared with consistent eyes-closed conditions under placebo, eyes-closed DMT is associated with striking changes in cortical dynamics, which are remarkably similar to those observed during actual eyes-open visual stimulation.
source: Results revealed that, compared with consistent eyes-closed conditions under placebo, eyes-closed DMT is associated with striking changes in cortical dynamics, which are remarkably similar to those observed during actual eyes-open visual stimulation (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Pang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Under DMT, we observed a reduction in backward waves, and increase in forward ones, as well as an overall decrease in α band (8–12 Hz) oscillatory frequencies.
source: Specifically, we observed a reduction in BW waves, and increase in FW ones, as well as an overall decrease in α band (8–12 Hz) oscillatory frequencies (Timmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: Increases in the amount of forward waves correlated positively with real-time ratings of the subjective intensity of the drug experience as well as post-hoc ratings of visual imagery.
source: Moreover, increases in the amount of FW waves correlated positively with real-time ratings of the subjective intensity of the drug experience as well as post-hoc ratings of visual imagery, suggesting a clear relationship between travelling waves and a distinct and novel type of conscious experience.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Previous work involving ayahuasca and BOLD fMRI found increased visual cortex BOLD signal under the drug vs placebo while participants engaged in an eyes-closed imagery task.
source: Previous work involving ayahuasca and BOLD fMRI found increased visual cortex BOLD signal under the drug vs placebo while participants engaged in an eyes-closed imagery task – a result that was interpreted as consistent with the 'visionary' effects of ayahuasca (de Araujo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: It is now generally accepted that occipital cortex becomes activated during visual imagery.
source: Despite some initial debate (Bartolomeo, 2008), it is now generally accepted that occipital cortex becomes activated during visual imagery (Fulford et al., 2018; Pearson, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research and represents established knowledge.

claim: DMT/ayahuasca – and perhaps other psychedelics – engage the visual apparatus in a fashion that is consistent with actual exogenously driven visual perception.
source: Placing these findings into the context of previous work demonstrating increased FW travelling waves during direct visual perception (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Pang et al., 2020), our present findings of increased FW waves under DMT correlating with visionary experiences lend significant support to the notion that DMT/ayahuasca – and perhaps other psychedelics – engage the visual apparatus in a fashion that is consistent with actual exogenously driven visual perception.
evidence: This is an inference combining current findings with previous research.

claim: As a classic serotonergic psychedelic drug, DMT's signature psychological effects are likely mediated by stimulation of the serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptor subtype.
source: As a classic serotonergic psychedelic drug, DMT's signature psychological effects are likely mediated by stimulation of the serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptor subtype.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about psychedelic pharmacology.

claim: The 5-HT2A receptor has been found to be essential for the full signature psychological and brain effects of Ayahuasca.
source: As with all other classic psychedelics (Nichols, 2016) the 5-HT2A receptor has been found to be essential for the full signature psychological and brain effects of Ayahuasca (Valle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The 5-HT2A receptor has been linked to visual hallucinations in neurological disorders.
source: In addition to its role in mediating altered perceptual experiences under psychedelics, the 5-HT2A receptor has also been linked to visual hallucinations in neurological disorders, with a 5-HT2A receptor inverse agonist having been licensed for hallucinations and delusions in Parkinson's disease with additional evidence for its efficacy in reducing consistent symptoms in Alzheimer's disease (Ballard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There is a wealth of evidence that Bayesian or predictive mechanisms play a fundamental role in cognitive and perceptual processing.
source: There is a wealth of evidence that Bayesian or predictive mechanisms play a fundamental role in cognitive and perceptual processing (den Ouden et al., 2012; Kok and De Lange, 2015) and our understanding of the functional architecture underlying such processing is continually being updated (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Friston, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: According to predictive coding, the brain strives to be a model of its environment.
source: According to predictive coding (Huang and Rao, 2011), the brain strives to be a model of its environment.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle supported by citation.

claim: Based on the assumption that the cortex is a hierarchical system, message passing from higher cortical levels is proposed to encode predictions about the activity of lower levels.
source: More specifically, based on the assumption that the cortex is a hierarchical system – message passing from higher cortical levels is proposed to encode predictions about the activity of lower levels.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle of predictive coding.

claim: When predictions are contradicted by the lower-level activity ('prediction error'), information passes up the cortical hierarchy where it can update predictions.
source: This mechanism is interrupted when predictions are contradicted by the lower-level activity ('prediction error') – in which case, information passes up the cortical hierarchy where it can update predictions.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle of predictive coding.

claim: Predictive coding has recently served as a guiding framework for explaining the psychological and functional brain effects of psychedelic compounds.
source: Predictive coding has recently served as a guiding framework for explaining the psychological and functional brain effects of psychedelic compounds (Carhart-Harris and Friston, 2019; Pink-Hashkes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent theoretical work.

claim: According to one model, psychedelics decrease the precision-weighting of top-down priors, thereby liberating bottom-up information flow.
source: According to one model (Carhart-Harris and Friston, 2019), psychedelics decrease the precision- weighting of top-down priors, thereby liberating bottom-up information flow.
evidence: This is a theoretical model supported by citation.

claim: Various aspects of the multi-level action of psychedelics are consistent with the model that psychedelics decrease the precision-weighting of top-down priors, such as the induction of asynchronous neuronal discharge rates in cortical layer 5, reduced alpha oscillations, increased signal complexity, and the breakdown of large-scale intrinsic networks.
source: Various aspects of the multi-level action of psychedelics are consistent with this model, such as the induction of asynchronous neuronal discharge rates in cortical layer 5 (Celada et al., 2008), reduced alpha oscillations (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013) increased signal complexity (Schartner et al., 2017; Timmermann et al., 2019) and the breakdown of large-scale intrinsic networks (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent empirically supported modelling work has lent support to assumptions that top-down predictions and bottom-up prediction-errors are encoded in the direction of propagating cortical travelling waves.
source: Recent empirically supported modelling work has lent support to assumptions that top-down predictions and bottom-up prediction-errors are encoded in the direction of propagating cortical travelling waves (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A minimal predictive coding model implementing biologically plausible constraints generates alpha-band travelling waves, which propagate from frontal to occipital regions and vice versa, depending on the 'cognitive states' of the model.
source: Specifically, these simulations demonstrated that a minimal predictive coding model implementing biologically plausible constraints (i.e. temporal delays in the communication between regions and time constants) generates alpha-band travelling waves, which propagate from frontal to occipital regions and vice versa, depending on the 'cognitive states' of the model (input-driven vs. prior-driven), as confirmed by EEG data in healthy participants (in that case, processing visual stimuli vs. closed-eyes resting state).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling and empirical work.

claim: Thirteen participants took part in this study (six females, age 34.4 ± 9.1 SD).
source: Thirteen participants took part in this study (six females, age 34.4 ± 9.1 SD), sample size was chosen based on prior EEG and MEG studies and effect sizes with similar compounds.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Sample size was chosen based on prior EEG and MEG studies and effect sizes with similar compounds.
source: Thirteen participants took part in this study (six females, age 34.4 ± 9.1 SD), sample size was chosen based on prior EEG and MEG studies and effect sizes with similar compounds.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on previous research.

claim: Participants attended two sessions, in the first one, they received placebo, while DMT was administered in the second session.
source: Participants attended two sessions, in the first one, they received placebo, while DMT was administered in the second session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A fixed-order, single blind design was employed considering that psychedelics have been shown to induce lasting psychological changes, which could have led to confounding effects on the following session if DMT had been administered in the first session.
source: We employed a fixed-order, single blind design considering that psychedelics have been shown to induce lasting psychological changes (Maclean et al., 2011), which could have led to confounding effects on the following session if DMT had been administered in the first session.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on previous research and inference about potential confounds.

claim: Progressively increasing doses of DMT were provided to different participants (four different doses were used: 7, 14, 18 and 20 mg, to 3, 4, 1, and 5 successive participants, respectively).
source: Given the lack of human data with DMT, progressively increasing doses were provided to different participants (four different doses were used: 7, 14, 18 and 20 mg, to 3, 4, 1, and 5 successive participants, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the dosing protocol.

claim: Participants rested in a semi-supine position with their eyes closed during the duration of the whole experiment.
source: Participants rested in a semi-supine position with their eyes closed during the duration of the whole experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: At each minute, participants provided an intensity rating.
source: At each minute, participants provided an intensity rating, while blood samples were taken at given time-points (the same for placebo and DMT conditions) via a cannula inserted in the participants' arm.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection procedure.

claim: One day after the DMT session, participants reported their subjective experience completing an interview composed of several questionnaires.
source: One day after the DMT session, participants reported their subjective experience completing an interview composed of several questionnaires (see Timmermann et al., 2019 for details).
evidence: This is a description of the data collection procedure.

claim: In this study we focused on the Visual Analogue Scale values.
source: In this study we focused on the Visual Analogue Scale values.
evidence: This is a description of which subjective measures were analyzed.

claim: EEG signals were recorded using a 32-channels Brainproduct EEG system sampling at 1000 Hz.
source: EEG signals were recorded using a 32-channels Brainproduct EEG system sampling at 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the recording equipment and parameters.

claim: The dominant natural propagation spread of travelling waves is along the axis that connects the furthest posterior and frontal recording channels.
source: This suggests that the dominant natural propagation spread of travelling waves is along the axis that connects the furthest posterior and frontal recording channels.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of different electrode arrays.

claim: Waves propagating from leftward to rightward regions (and vice versa), were not affected by DMT.
source: As a control, we additionally demonstrated that waves propagating from leftward to rightward regions (and vice versa), were not affected by DMT (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: An additional analysis based on relative phases of the alpha band-pass signals over all channels confirmed that DMT disrupts the typical top-down propagation of alpha-band waves.
source: Besides, in-line with previous work on travelling waves (Alexander et al., 2013; Alexander et al., 2006), an additional analysis based on relative phases of the alpha band-pass signals over all channels, confirmed the same results, with DMT indeed disrupting the typical top-down propagation of alpha-band waves.
evidence: This is supported by additional analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: DMT induces an overall decrease of spectral power, especially in the alpha band backward waves.
source: Due to DMT, we observed overall a large reduction in absolute power, in-line with previous results.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In travelling wave systems, waves occur in groups (or packets) over some range of spatial wavelengths having multiple spatial and temporal frequencies.
source: As demonstrated by both theoretical and experimental evidence (Nunez, 2000; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2014; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2009), in most systems, including the human brain, travelling waves occur in groups (or packets) over some range of spatial wavelengths having multiple spatial and temporal frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Given any configurations of electrodes, only parts of wave packets can be successfully detected, i.e. waves shorter than the spatial extent of the array, and waves longer than twice the electrode separation distance (Nyquist criterion in space).
source: Given any configurations of electrodes, only parts of these packets can be successfully detected, i.e. waves shorter than the spatial extent of the array, and waves longer than twice the electrode separation distance (Nyquist criterion in space).
evidence: This is based on established principles of signal processing and measurement.

claim: In scalp recordings, the shorter waves may be mostly removed by volume conduction.
source: In scalp recordings, the shorter waves may be mostly removed by volume conduction.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEG recording limitations.

claim: Waves recorded directly from the cortex emphasize shorter waves than the scalp recorded waves.
source: As a consequence, waves recorded directly from the cortex emphasize shorter waves than the scalp recorded waves.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about differences between cortical and scalp recordings.

claim: In the case of small cortical arrays, the overlap between cortical and scalp data may be minimal, and the estimated wave properties (including propagation direction) may differ.
source: Specifically, in the case of small cortical arrays, the overlap between cortical and scalp data may be minimal, and the estimated wave properties (including propagation direction) may differ.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about measurement differences.

claim: When waves are travelling in multiple directions at nearly the same time in 'closed' systems (e.g. the cortical/white matter), waves either damp out or interfere with each other to form standing waves.
source: Additionally, it is important to consider that when waves are travelling in multiple directions at nearly the same time in 'closed' systems (e.g. the cortical/white matter), waves either damp out or interfere with each other to form standing waves (e.g. alpha waves travelling both forward and backward).
